1Pembuka Unit — “What If Magic Happened on Our Island?”

Bayangkan suasana sore di sebuah pulau kecil. Angin laut bertiup pelan. Perahu-perahu mulai kembali ke dermaga. Langit berwarna jingga, dan beberapa siswa duduk di depan rumah sambil mendengarkan cerita dari nenek mereka.

“Long ago, there was a golden shell that could speak when the moon touched the sea.”

Seorang siswa bertanya:

“What if the fairy tale happened on our island?”

Pertanyaan itu membuat semua orang terdiam. Mereka mulai membayangkan sebuah dongeng: seorang anak pulau yang menemukan benda ajaib, seorang pedagang serakah yang ingin mengambilnya, sebuah gua rahasia di bawah tebing, dan suara laut yang menyimpan janji lama.

Dalam unit ini, kamu akan belajar bahwa fairy tale is not only about magic. Dongeng bukan hanya tentang peri, penyihir, istana, atau benda ajaib. Dongeng juga dapat mengajarkan nilai hidup: keberanian, kejujuran, kebijaksanaan, tanggung jawab, dan kepedulian kepada lingkungan.

Opening hook: storytelling, island context, and childhood fairy tales.

Pertanyaan Pemantik

  1. What fairy tale did you hear when you were a child?
  2. Who told you the story?
  3. What magical thing happened in the story?
  4. Who was the good character?
  1. Who was the bad character?
  2. What lesson did you learn?
  3. Can a fairy tale teach us about real life?
  4. If a fairy tale happened on your island, what magical object might appear?
Catatan: Instruksi dan pengantar materi menggunakan Bahasa Indonesia agar mudah dipahami, tetapi latihan utama tetap mengarahkan kamu menggunakan Bahasa Inggris.

2Tujuan Pembelajaran dan Alur Belajar

Tujuan Pembelajaran

Setelah mempelajari unit ini, kamu diharapkan mampu:

  1. menjelaskan fungsi sosial fairy tale sebagai teks naratif;
  2. mengidentifikasi struktur teks fairy tale: orientation, complication, sequence of events, resolution, dan moral value;
  3. menganalisis tokoh protagonis dan antagonis dalam dongeng;
  4. mengidentifikasi konflik utama dan penyelesaian dalam cerita;
  5. menemukan nilai moral dalam fairy tale;
  6. memahami dan menggunakan adjectives untuk mendeskripsikan tokoh, benda, dan latar;
  1. membentuk noun phrases yang rinci dan alami dalam Bahasa Inggris;
  2. menganalisis fairy tale yang dimodifikasi dari sudut pandang berbeda;
  3. menyimak narasi dongeng modern dan mengklasifikasikan sifat karakter berdasarkan informasi audio;
  4. menulis alternative ending dari sebuah fairy tale secara kreatif;
  5. melakukan role-play berdasarkan karakter dongeng yang telah dimodifikasi;
  6. merefleksikan kesulitan dalam menyusun kalimat deskriptif menggunakan noun phrases.

4Concept Exploration — What Is a Fairy Tale?

Infografis: definition, common elements, social functions, and text structure of fairy tales.

A fairy tale is an imaginative story that usually includes magical events, magical characters, impossible situations, or wonderful transformations. Fairy tales are often told to entertain people and teach moral lessons.

Dalam Bahasa Indonesia, fairy tale dapat dipahami sebagai dongeng fantasi yang mengandung unsur keajaiban dan biasanya memiliki pesan moral.

A. Common Elements of Fairy Tales

ElementExplanationExample
Magical characterA character with magical powerfairy, witch, wizard, mermaid, sea spirit
Magical objectAn object with special powergolden shell, magic mirror, enchanted ring
TransformationA magical changea fish becomes a prince
ConflictThe main problemcurse, jealousy, greed, broken promise
Good vs evilA struggle between good and bad choicesa brave girl vs a greedy merchant
Journey or testA challenge for the herocrossing a stormy sea, solving riddles
Moral valueThe lesson of the storyDo not be greedy; keep your promise

B. Fairy Tale vs Legend vs Myth vs Fable

TypeCharacteristicsExample
Fairy TaleMagical, imaginative, often good vs evilCinderella, Snow White
LegendConnected to a place or local belief; sometimes believed as true by a communityThe Legend of Toba Lake
MythRelated to gods, creation, or supernatural beliefscreation myths
FableUses animals as main characters and teaches moral lessonThe Tortoise and the Hare

C. Common Settings in Fairy Tales

a faraway kingdoman ancient foresta mysterious islanda lonely beacha hidden cavea small fishing villagea wooden house near the shorea coral palace under the seaa silent lagoona broken pier under the moonlight

Example sentence:

Long ago, on a quiet island surrounded by bright blue water, there lived a kind-hearted girl named Lila.

5Social Function of Fairy Tales

A. To Entertain

Fairy tales make readers imagine wonderful and impossible things.

Example: A talking fish appeared from the silver waves and gave the boy a tiny golden key.

B. To Teach Moral Values

Fairy tales teach readers about good and bad choices.

Example: The greedy merchant lost everything because he broke his promise.

C. To Preserve Cultural Imagination

Fairy tales keep stories, values, and imagination alive from one generation to another.

Example: A grandmother tells a story about a magical shell to remind children to respect the sea.

D. To Warn People

Fairy tales warn readers about greed, arrogance, cruelty, dishonesty, or carelessness.

Example: The boy entered the forbidden cave because he was arrogant, and he almost never returned.

E. To Inspire Hope

Fairy tales often show that ordinary people can become brave and wise.

Example: The youngest daughter, who was often ignored, saved the village with her honesty.

6Text Structure of Fairy Tales

Fairy tales are narrative texts. They usually have the following structure.

1. Orientation

Orientation introduces characters, place, and time.

Guiding questions: Who is the story about? Where does the story happen? When does the story happen? What is the situation at the beginning?

Example: Once upon a time, there lived a brave young girl on a small island near the eastern sea.

2. Complication

Complication introduces the problem or conflict.

Guiding questions: What problem happens? Who causes the problem? Why does the problem become serious?

Example: One night, a greedy merchant arrived and tried to steal the magical shell that protected the island.

3. Sequence of Events

This part shows what happens after the problem begins.

Guiding questions: What does the main character do? What challenges appear? How does the conflict become more intense?

Example: The girl followed the glowing footprints to a dark cave under the cliff.

4. Resolution

Resolution shows how the problem is solved.

Guiding questions: How is the problem solved? What happens to the protagonist? What happens to the antagonist?

Example: The shell broke the curse, and the storm stopped before it destroyed the village.

5. Moral Value / Coda

This part gives the lesson of the story.

Guiding questions: What lesson can readers learn? What value is shown through the ending?

Example: Since that day, the villagers learned that nature protects those who protect it.

8Grammar Focus — Adjectives and Noun Phrases

Infografis: adjective position, noun phrase pattern, adjective order, examples, and common mistakes.

A. What Is an Adjective?

An adjective is a word that describes a noun.

NounAdjective + Noun
girla brave girl
seathe stormy sea
cavea dark cave
shella golden shell
witcha cruel witch
grandmothera wise grandmother
villagea peaceful village
mirrora cursed mirror

C. Position of Adjectives

Before a noun: a brave girl, a mysterious cave, a greedy merchant, a magical shell.

After linking verbs: The girl was brave. The cave looked mysterious. The merchant became greedy. The shell seemed magical.

D. What Is a Noun Phrase?

A noun phrase is a group of words built around a noun. It gives more information about a person, place, thing, or idea.

Start simple: shell → a shell → a golden shell → a tiny golden shell → a tiny golden shell from the silent island → a tiny golden shell from the silent island that could speak under the moonlight.

E. Noun Phrase Pattern

Determiner + adjective(s) + noun + extra information

Example: a mysterious old wooden box under the bed

10Reading Text 1 — The Golden Shell of the Silent Island

Bacalah dongeng berikut dengan saksama. Perhatikan tokoh, konflik, latar, benda ajaib, dan pesan moralnya.

Reading image: Arman finds a glowing golden shell on a quiet beach at dusk.

The Golden Shell of the Silent Island

Long ago, on a small island surrounded by clear blue water, there lived a humble student named Arman. He was not the strongest boy in his village, and he was not the richest. His father was a fisherman, and his mother sold dried seaweed near the small wooden pier. Every morning, Arman walked to school with a worn-out bag, a pair of dusty sandals, and a quiet smile.

Although his life was simple, Arman had one special habit. After school, he always cleaned the beach near his house. He picked up broken plastic cups, old ropes, and food wrappers left by careless visitors. His friends sometimes laughed at him.

“Why do you clean the beach every day?” asked Riko, his classmate.

Arman smiled and answered, “The sea gives us fish, rain, stories, and journeys. If we do not respect it, how can we ask it to protect us?”

One evening, after a long day at school, Arman walked along the shore. The sky was purple, and the waves touched the sand softly. Suddenly, he saw a tiny golden shell shining between two black stones. It was not an ordinary shell. It glowed gently, as if a small star had fallen from the sky and chosen to sleep on the beach.

Arman picked it up carefully.

Then, a soft voice whispered, “Do not sell me. Do not hide me. Return me when the moon stands above the sea.”

Arman almost dropped the shell. He looked around, but no one was there.

“Who are you?” he asked.

“I am the Golden Shell of the Silent Island,” the voice replied. “For many years, I have protected this village from storms. But I can only protect those who keep their promises.”

Arman was frightened, but he was also curious. He put the shell inside his pocket and ran home. That night, he told his grandmother everything.

His grandmother’s face became serious.

“When I was young,” she said, “my grandmother told me about a magical golden shell. It belonged to the sea spirit. It protected the island because our ancestors promised to keep the shore clean and never take more from the sea than they needed.”

Arman touched the shell in his pocket. It felt warm.

“What should I do?” he asked.

“Return it to the Moon Cave before midnight,” said his grandmother. “The cave is under the cliff, behind the old coconut tree. But be careful. Magic often attracts greed.”

The next morning, news about the golden shell spread through the village. Arman did not know who had told the story, but many people came to his house. Some wanted to see the shell. Some wanted to touch it. Some wanted to borrow it for luck.

Among them was a rich merchant named Mr. Badrun. He had arrived on the island two days earlier with a large motorboat and five workers. He bought sea cucumbers, dried fish, and shells from villagers. He smiled politely, but his eyes always counted profit.

“My dear boy,” said Mr. Badrun, “I heard you found a rare shell. I will buy it for five million rupiah.”

Arman shook his head. “It is not for sale.”

“Ten million,” said the merchant.

“No,” answered Arman.

The merchant’s smile disappeared for a second, but he quickly laughed. “You are young. You do not understand value. With that money, your family can buy many things.”

“My grandmother said I must return it,” Arman replied.

Mr. Badrun stepped closer. “Stories from old people are only stories. Gold is real.”

Arman looked at the shell. It no longer felt warm. It felt cold, as if it were afraid.

That evening, dark clouds gathered above the sea. The wind moved strangely, and the waves became restless. Arman knew he had to go to the Moon Cave. He wrapped the golden shell in a piece of clean cloth and walked toward the cliff.

Riko saw him and followed.

“Are you really going to the cave?” Riko asked.

“Yes,” said Arman. “I made a promise.”

“But the sky is getting dark.”

“A promise is still a promise, even when the sky is dark.”

The two boys walked through a narrow path behind the cliff. The wind became stronger. Coconut leaves shook above them like frightened hands. When they reached the old coconut tree, they saw a dark opening under the rock. It was the Moon Cave.

Inside the cave, the air smelled of wet stones and salt. The walls shone faintly, covered with tiny crystals. At the end of the cave, there was a small pool of seawater. Moonlight entered through a hole in the ceiling and touched the surface of the pool.

Arman stepped forward.

Suddenly, a voice shouted, “Stop!”

Mr. Badrun appeared behind them with a lantern in his hand. His face looked different now. There was no polite smile, only hunger.

“Give me the shell,” he said.

Arman held the cloth tightly. “No. It belongs to the sea.”

“It belongs to whoever can use it,” Mr. Badrun said. “With that shell, I can sell magic to tourists. I can become famous.”

Riko whispered, “Arman, let’s run.”

But the merchant’s workers blocked the entrance.

The golden shell began to glow. The cave trembled. Outside, thunder rolled across the sky.

Mr. Badrun grabbed Arman’s arm. “Give it to me!”

Arman struggled. The shell fell from the cloth and landed near the pool. Everyone stared at it.

Then the soft voice returned, but this time it filled the cave.

“Human hearts are tested not when they are poor, but when they see a chance to take what is not theirs.”

Mr. Badrun stepped back. “Who said that?”

The water in the pool rose slowly and formed the shape of a tall woman made of moonlight and sea foam. Her hair flowed like dark waves, and her eyes shone like stars reflected on water.

“I am the guardian of this island,” she said. “For many years, I protected this village because people respected the sea. But greed has entered this shore.”

Mr. Badrun fell to his knees. “I only wanted to make business.”

“Business without respect becomes destruction,” said the sea guardian.

The cave shook again. A large wave crashed outside the cliff. Riko cried out in fear.

Arman picked up the shell and walked toward the pool. His hands were shaking, but his voice was clear.

“I return this shell to the sea,” he said. “I do not want money from it. I only ask you to protect our village.”

The golden shell floated above his hands. Then it moved slowly into the pool. The moonlight became brighter. The wind outside suddenly stopped. The thunder disappeared. The sea became calm again.

The sea guardian looked at Arman.

“You kept your promise,” she said. “Because of your honesty, the island will be protected. But remember this: magic cannot save people who keep destroying what they have.”

Then she turned to Mr. Badrun.

“You will not be punished with death,” she said. “You will be punished with memory. Every time you see the sea, you will remember what greed almost destroyed.”

Mr. Badrun cried. For the first time, he looked small and tired.

The next morning, the villagers found the beach cleaner than ever. The storm had not destroyed a single house. Mr. Badrun left the island quietly, but before leaving, he paid the villagers fairly and returned the shells he had taken from protected areas.

Arman continued going to school with his worn-out bag and dusty sandals. But something changed. His friends no longer laughed when he cleaned the beach. Riko joined him. Then other students joined too.

Years later, people still told the story of the Golden Shell of the Silent Island. Some said it was only a fairy tale. Others said that on certain nights, when the moon stood above the sea, a tiny golden light could still be seen under the waves.

But Arman never argued. He only smiled and said, “The sea remembers. So should we.”

Climax image: the Moon Cave, golden shell, sea guardian, and the greedy merchant.

11Reading Text 2 — The Witch’s Side of the Story

Bacalah teks berikut. Cerita ini menggunakan sudut pandang tokoh yang biasanya dianggap jahat.

The Witch’s Side of the Story

People always call me the wicked witch.

They say I lived in a dark old house at the edge of the forest. They say I frightened children, cursed travelers, and laughed when people cried. But people enjoy simple stories. They like heroes who shine and villains who are easy to hate.

My story was not simple.

Many years ago, I was not a witch. I was a healer. I lived in a small wooden house near a quiet river. People came to me when their children were sick, when their fields were dry, or when their hearts were broken. I used leaves, roots, warm water, and old songs my mother had taught me.

One winter, the king’s son became ill. The palace guards took me to the castle. I stayed awake for three nights beside the prince. I made bitter medicine from silver leaves and mountain flowers. On the fourth morning, the prince opened his eyes.

The king smiled and said, “Ask for anything.”

I asked for one thing only: “Protect the forest. The medicine that saved your son grows there.”

The king promised.

But kings forget promises when gold speaks louder than wisdom. A year later, soldiers cut down the forest to build a larger palace. The river became muddy. The silver leaves disappeared. The mountain flowers died.

When I protested, people called me dangerous. When I cried, they called me dramatic. When I used my remaining magic to protect the last tree, they called me a witch.

So I left.

I built a small house deep in the remaining forest. I made the walls dark so hunters would stay away. I hung bones above the door, not to frighten children, but to warn greedy adults. I created illusions, not to harm travelers, but to protect the last living roots under the ground.

Then one day, a young girl came to my house. She was lost, hungry, and afraid. I gave her warm soup. I let her sleep near the fire. But when she returned to her village, people asked where she had been.

“At the witch’s house,” she said.

After that, the story grew teeth.

They said I trapped children. They said I ate them. They said my soup was poison.

No one asked the girl whether I had saved her.

Now, when people tell fairy tales, they call me evil. They do not mention the broken promise, the dying forest, or the king who took everything and still remained noble in their songs.

Maybe I am not innocent. Anger changed me. Loneliness sharpened my voice. Pain made me suspicious.

But before you call someone a monster, ask what turned them into one.

Activities

A. Point of View Analysis

  5. Why did people misunderstand the witch?
  6. What moral value can readers learn?

B. Noun Phrase Hunt

Examples: a dark old house; a small wooden house; bitter medicine; silver leaves; the last living roots; warm soup; the broken promise; the dying forest.

Now write five new noun phrases to describe the witch.

12Listening Section — The Mermaid Who Refused the Crown

Listening Script

Long ago, under the clear water near a chain of small islands, there was a kingdom of mermaids. The palace was made of coral walls, pearl windows, and glowing blue stones. In that kingdom lived Princess Marena, the youngest daughter of the Sea Queen.

Marena was different from her sisters. Her sisters loved golden crowns, royal songs, and long ceremonies. Marena loved swimming near fishing boats, listening to human stories, and helping lost sailors find their way home.

One day, the Sea Queen called Marena to the throne room.

“My daughter,” said the queen, “the time has come. You must wear the crown and rule the southern sea.”

Marena looked at the crown. It was beautiful, but it felt heavy even before she touched it.

“Mother,” she said softly, “I am not ready to rule from a throne.”

The queen frowned. “A princess does not refuse duty.”

“I am not refusing duty,” Marena replied. “I am refusing a crown that will keep me away from the people who need help.”

The royal guards whispered. Her sisters stared at her in shock.

That night, a violent storm struck the islands above. A small wooden boat was thrown between high waves. Inside the boat were three students, a father, and a grandmother. They had been returning from another island when the weather suddenly changed.

Marena heard their cries.

Without waiting for permission, she swam toward the surface. The storm was dangerous. The waves were huge, and lightning cut the sky. Marena pushed the boat away from the rocks. She sang an old sea song, and the waves slowly followed her voice.

By morning, the boat reached a safe shore.

The Sea Queen was angry at first. “You left the palace during the royal ceremony!”

Marena answered, “Yes, Mother. Because leadership is not only sitting on a throne. Leadership is listening when people are afraid.”

The Sea Queen became silent. She looked at the crown in her hands. For many years, she had believed that a ruler must stay above others. But Marena showed her another truth.

The next day, the queen did not force Marena to wear the crown. Instead, she gave her a smaller silver necklace shaped like a wave.

“This is not a crown,” said the queen. “It is a promise. Serve the sea in your own way.”

Since that day, Marena became known not as the queen of the southern sea, but as the guardian of lost boats. Fishermen said that when the night was dark and the waves were high, a gentle voice could sometimes be heard between the wind and the water.

It was Marena, guiding people home.

14Writing Section — Alternative Ending

Writing infographic: steps and checklist for writing an alternative ending.

An alternative ending is a new ending created by changing the original ending of a story.

Kamu dapat mengubah: keputusan tokoh; hasil konflik; pesan moral; sudut pandang; nasib tokoh antagonis; peran tokoh yang dianggap lemah.

Writing Topic: Rewrite the ending of a fairy tale so that the weakest character becomes the wisest character.

A. Writing Steps

Step 1: Choose a fairy tale

Examples: Cinderella, Snow White, The Little Mermaid, Hansel and Gretel, Beauty and the Beast, Timun Mas, Bawang Merah and Bawang Putih, a local fairy tale from your community.

Step 2: Identify the original ending

Ask: How does the original story end? Who wins? Who loses? What lesson is shown?

Step 3: Decide what to change

You may change: the villain becomes regretful; the weak character becomes wise; the magical object is destroyed; the protagonist chooses forgiveness; the ending becomes more realistic; the moral lesson becomes deeper.

Step 4: Change the character’s decision

Original: The prince saved the princess.

Alternative: The princess saved herself by solving the witch’s riddle.

Step 5: Add a new problem or twist

Example: The golden crown looked beautiful, but it slowly erased the memory of anyone who wore it.

Step 6: Create a meaningful resolution

Example: Instead of wearing the crown, the youngest daughter returned it to the sea and chose to protect her village.

Step 7: Add moral value

Example: Wisdom is not always found in the strongest person. Sometimes, it grows quietly in the person no one notices.

B. Writing Planner

PartYour Notes
Title of original fairy tale
Original ending
Character you want to change
New problem/twist
New decision
New ending
Moral value
Adjectives you will use
Noun phrases you will use

C. Sentence Starters

FunctionSentence Starters
StartingIn the original story,… / However, in my version,…
Showing conflictSuddenly,… / Unfortunately,… / The problem became worse when…
Showing decisionAfter thinking deeply,… / Although she/he was afraid,…
Showing resolutionIn the end,… / Since that day,…
Showing moral valueThe story teaches us that… / From that moment, everyone learned that…

D. Model Alternative Ending

In the original story, the youngest sister waited for someone to save her. However, in my version, she did not wait. When the cruel queen locked her inside a dark narrow tower, she listened carefully to the sound of the wind. She noticed that the wind always entered from a small broken window near the roof.

Using a thin silver hairpin, she opened the old wooden window and called a tiny blue bird that often visited her. The bird carried her message to the village. But the message was not a request for revenge. It was a warning.

“Do not attack the palace,” she wrote. “The queen is not powerful without the magic mirror.”

That night, the villagers came silently. The youngest sister walked into the throne room and spoke to the queen. “You are not hated because you are old,” she said. “You are feared because you are cruel.”

The queen looked into the cursed mirror and saw not beauty, but loneliness. She dropped the mirror, and it broke into a hundred pieces of cold glass.

Since that day, the youngest sister became known not as the weakest child, but as the wisest voice in the kingdom.

E. Independent Writing Task

Write your alternative ending in 250–350 words.

Your writing must include: at least 10 adjectives; at least 6 noun phrases; at least 5 time connectors; past tense; dialogue; a clear conflict; a meaningful resolution; a moral value.

F. Writing Checklist

CriteriaYesNeeds Revision
I changed the original ending creatively.
I used past tense correctly.
I used at least 10 adjectives.
I used at least 6 noun phrases.
I used time connectors.
I included dialogue.
I showed a clear moral value.
My ending is coherent and meaningful.

Setting: A small wooden pier at night.

Arman: What are you doing here, Sir? The boats have already left.

Merchant: I am looking for a tiny golden shell. People say it shines under the moonlight.

Arman: Money cannot protect our island from a broken promise.

Talking Fish: The sea is listening.

Grandmother: Choose wisely. A small decision can create a large wave.

Merchant: I… I only wanted to become rich.

Arman: Then learn this: wealth without respect will leave you empty.

Writing Performance Task

Write an alternative ending of a fairy tale in 250–350 words. Your alternative ending must include: a clear connection to the original fairy tale; a changed decision or changed fate; at least one meaningful conflict; at least one dialogue; at least 10 adjectives; at least 6 noun phrases; at least 5 time connectors; past tense; and a clear moral value.

Suggested titles: The Mermaid Who Chose the Island; The Witch Who Protected the Forest; The Prince Who Returned the Crown; The Youngest Child and the Golden Shell; The Giant Who Learned to Listen; The Talking Fish and the Broken Promise.

Speaking Performance Task

Perform a modified fairy tale role-play in groups of 4–6 students. Duration: 5–7 minutes. Your performance must include: a clear setting; modified fairy tale characters; a magical object or magical event; a conflict; dialogue among characters; a resolution; a moral value; at least five noun phrases used orally.

21Final Student Mission

You are now a fairy tale writer.

Your mission is to create a meaningful fairy tale ending that speaks to your own life and community.

  • Magic makes the story interesting.
  • Conflict makes the story move.
  • Character choices make the story meaningful.
  • Noun phrases make the story vivid.
  • Moral value makes the story stay in people’s hearts.
  • Write with imagination. Speak with confidence. Reflect with honesty.

The sea has stories.
The island has stories.
Your voice can retell them in English.
